text-style-readable-minimum.headline: The most contested provision in the draft: what counts as readable text, how to measure it, and in which unit.

positions.label: Testability first
positions.detail: A requirement is only useful if authors can apply it and two testers reach the same verdict. CSS px is defensible as the anchor because it is defined by visual angle rather than physical pixels, so it is device-independent. Browser zoom — the default control, persistent across sites — is the user's route to larger text, so a minimum size plus available magnification is judged sufficient.

positions.label: The metric does not measure the thing
positions.detail: CSS font-size is a poor proxy for legibility: x-height and stroke weight vary enormously between typefaces at the same nominal size, and rendering differs by OS and font cut. sdw32 points to the EN 301 549 draft, which gives an x-height of at least 8 CSS px for the smallest text as best practice, and proposes handling weight by pixel density rather than the binary normal/bold split. Myndex argues a test that is merely testable, without being useful, gets codified into law with unintended consequences. Myndex nonetheless defends the CSS px, defined by visual angle, as the right reference unit for guidelines, with x-height rather than font-size as the measure.

positions.label: User autonomy over layout stability
positions.detail: px ignores a user's configured root font size while rem respects it, so anchoring the standard in px effectively tells the market that overriding user preference is acceptable. chaals lands in the middle: provide both a baseline that conveys a commonly legible absolute size and clear guidance that resizing must actually work — and reports from browsing ~100 pages at 64px that most sites, news sites especially, become unusable, which he attributed mainly to layouts set in pixels.

positions.label: Style wording needs revision
positions.detail: "Does not use a decorative or cursive font face" is called subjective and over-broad. Finnberrys, a voice-recognition user, wants underlining restricted to links because randomly underlined text repeatedly reads as a link. julierawe wants "most text" defined before the requirement can be tested.

positions.label: Validate beyond Latin scripts
positions.detail: x-height does not translate to Japanese, Chinese or Korean, so any text-appearance metric has to be checked against non-Latin writing systems before it ships in a global standard.

agreed: No one defended WCAG 2's binary normal/bold font-weight classification. TestPartners noted weight 600 is common in practice and said that if the binary is kept the spec must say how intermediate values are treated; patrickhlauke, Myndex and sdw32 went further, arguing the nominal CSS weight value is not a reliable measure across typefaces.
Any size metric has to be density-neutral, not "as measured on screen", because authors cannot control or test physical rendering.
detlevhfischer and Myndex both found the "decorative or cursive font face" wording too restrictive to stand as a requirement; no one in the thread defended it.

No one disputed GreggVan's point that a requirement need not be machine-testable as long as it is objective enough for different evaluators to reach the same conclusion, though Myndex countered that testability alone is not helpful if the test lacks utility.
open: Whether there is any minimum size requirement for default text presentation at all. sdw32 registered deep concern that it was removed; GreggVan's position is that if a size is legible for typical vision, OS magnification covers low vision. chaals also argued WCAG should state a reasonable default text size; alastc pointed to the editor's draft Text style readable (minimum) provision, at a fairly small equivalent of 10pt, as that baseline. In #407 solhell proposed raising the minimum to 12pt, GreggVan replied that this mixes up minimum and body text size, and hidde asked that authors not be forced to set a size at all.
px versus rem versus x-height as the anchoring unit.

Whether APCA replaces the 4.5:1 contrast ratio. sydneycolemanfromgoogle challenged the disruption to tooling, design systems and existing UIs and asked for research showing the benefit outweighs it. Myndex replied that the WCAG 2 ratio produces false passes and fails, that tooling changes are small, and that the working group has not committed to any specific replacement.
Whether accessible typeface guidance belongs in WCAG 3 at all, given there is no CSS-queryable way to assess a font and font choice is effectively unbounded (issue #245).
text-style-readable-minimum.note: Issue #642 became contentious enough that the chair stepped in to clarify that GitHub threads are individual discussion, not a formal working-group response channel. alastc, as a chair, later drafted a response for the AG group proposing to close #642 without change, noting WCAG 3 does not use px or rem values for text-sizing; graphic-designer objected and the draft awaits group consensus.

text-reflow-supported.headline: Whether WCAG 3 should anchor sizing in CSS px or rem, and how far text-only resizing has to work.

positions.label: CSS px is already relative
positions.detail: CSS px is relative to assumed viewing distance, which is what lets a requirement say how large something must appear across platforms. alastc notes WCAG 3 does not currently use px or rem for text sizing at all, and drafted a response proposing the issue be closed without changing any provision. GreggVan argues rem only says how big something is relative to something else, so an accessibility requirement cannot be written in rem because it sets no minimum size, and adds that px has only ever been cited as a minimum, not a fixed size. Myndex adds that the CSS px is defined as a unit of visual angle, the measure vision and readability science uses, while em and rem have no fixed relationship to it; using rem in practice is fine, but guidelines should trace to visual angle.

positions.label: rem respects the user, px does not
positions.detail: A user who sets a larger default font size sees rem-based layouts adapt and px-based layouts stay rigid. Argues this makes px a technical regression against user autonomy, and that calling it a user-agent problem shifts responsibility away from the standard.

positions.label: Both, and widen the resize range
positions.detail: Neither layout stability nor user scalability is the goal — people being able to read what is published is. Tested the disputed demo across Vivaldi, Avast, Safari and Firefox and found the px box adapts in some Chromium builds and not others, so the behaviour is not uniform. On the unit question itself he leans toward rem: asked whether px makes sense as a core unit for layouts rather than rem, his answer is "generally not"; he tells GreggVan an accessibility statement based on rem is perfectly feasible; and after browsing about 100 pages at a 64px font size he traced most serious problems to layouts set in pixels, concluding that promoting rem instead of px would really help. He also wants a reasonable default text size stated. Proposes a separate issue: content should support text-size adjustment well beyond the current 100–200% range.

positions.label: Density is the user's call, not the author's
positions.detail: On the related question of high-DPI viewports, raised in #156 by PAFaieta, who suggested a baseline native resolution and DPI or a baseline minimum magnification such as 200%, patrickhlauke replies that authors cannot predict or test the physical resolution a user runs, so a guideline cannot introduce that variability. A user running a small monitor at very high resolution has made that choice and can adapt their device.

agreed: Zoom currently works better across real sites than text-only resizing — alastc's claim, which chaals accepted ("Yes, zoom works better in most sites than increased text-size"), while calling his own survey anecdotal and attributing the breakage it found to layouts set in pixels.
Large headings scaling proportionally is a real layout problem, which is why the draft asks for 200% of default body size rather than 200% of starting size.
open: Whether content must support text-size adjustment beyond 200%.
Whether the spec should state a reasonable, commonly legible default text size.
Whether px-based layouts breaking under user font scaling is an author obligation or a user-agent gap.

Whether provisions should be written as regulation-ready requirements or as guidance grounded in common practice — GreggVan says outcomes are shalls that regulators must be able to use, while chaals says the group's only formal authority is to develop guidance.
alastc's draft response has not been through the group, so the issue is not resolved.

no-visual-motion.headline: Whether honouring prefers-reduced-motion can satisfy the requirement, and whether motion harm belongs at the base level rather than as an optional extra.

positions.label: Not hurting users should be the floor
positions.detail: The WCAG 2 equivalent sits at AAA, which in practice means it is ignored. If a user has set prefers-reduced-motion, respecting it should be required, not aspirational. guyhickling argues a mechanism to stop animation is no help when the harm lands before the user reaches the control — particularly for keyboard users.

positions.label: "Reduced" is not "none"
positions.detail: prefers-reduced-motion is a single binary flag, but users are usually affected by specific kinds of motion, and the setting is sometimes enabled accidentally. Treating it as "turn off all animation" is too draconian for a normative requirement and risks developers writing WCAG off entirely.

positions.label: The group has stalled on measurement before
positions.detail: Defining size and duration across devices and zoom levels is where this previously broke down, and duration is undefined when the motion is triggered by user action such as scrolling. Moving it to a base level requires evidence of impact at a given size and speed, and a consensus process means persuading those who objected last time.

positions.label: The evidence cannot ethically be gathered
positions.detail: A study demonstrating harm from motion would harm its participants. Also argues the need is broader than vestibular illness: hyper-vigilance and attention impairments mean even small, sub-second animation costs time and mental energy to recover from. alastc replied that such a study need not force anyone to view animations — participants could log the animations they encounter and the symptoms triggered — and that whether there is an impact is believed and understood; the question is what specifically triggers symptoms.

agreed: That motion causes real harm to some users is not in dispute: alastc, who brought the WCAG 2.1 criterion, says the impact is believed and understood, and patrickhlauke's objection is to the breadth of the remedy, not the need. The disagreement is over what specifically triggers symptoms and where to draw the line.
open: Whether a user preference can be relied on to satisfy the requirement at all. In #629 alastc asked this of the flashing note and said it applies equally to reduced motion; julierawe called it dangerous for flashing, asking what happens when someone looks at another person's device, and alastc doubts such a preference is accessibility supported today.

How to define a size and duration threshold that is testable without a screen ruler, which patrickhlauke raised as a reductio and mgifford answered by pointing out 4.5:1 looked equally arbitrary in 2008.

Whether "pseudo-motion" should get examples in its definition and its own provision. julierawe filed #739 for the COGA Task Force proposing parallax scrolling, sharp colour changes, dynamically updating content and others, and asking that No pseudo-motion stand alone so it cannot be read as allowed under 5 seconds; rachaelbradley suggested the decoy font as a possible example, mraccess77 said it gives him a headache, and julierawe added gamma-oscillation and sliced images. No one has responded for the group.

Whether small animations are triggers. alastc said the WCAG 2.1 work found small animations such as icons changing on hover were not, so a minimum size seemed necessary; mraccess77 replied that jiggling icons do impact some users and supplied a live example.

Whether the Windows reduced-motion switch is too coarse. mraccess77 reports it blocks animations they want along with those they do not and wants finer control, whereas CharlesBelov and guyhickling treat the on/off switch as a clear statement that animation should stop.

Whether the time limits for auto-playing audio (3 seconds) and moving or auto-updating content (5 seconds) should be unified. Wildebrew asked in #181 and recommended folding the auto-playing audio requirement into 2.2.2's equivalent; when alastc floated increasing 1.4.2's time instead, Wildebrew backed 5 seconds and asked that WCAG 3 group all page-level animation and sound together. alastc and bruce-usab were reluctant to change it within 2.x, and bruce-usab noted three seconds for both would also be logical.
julierawe's separate objection (#733) that naming the guideline "Avoid Physical Harm" excludes the cognitive harm — lost focus, fatigue, re-orientation cost — that motion also causes.

no-flashing-over-threshold.headline: Whether the flash size threshold has to hold under magnification, and whether user preferences or warnings can stand in for the requirement.

positions.label: Zoom must be accounted for
positions.detail: WCAG's philosophy is that criteria hold simultaneously, so a user who needs magnification must still be protected from seizure triggers; on a phone, 470 CSS px is most of the screen already. WilcoFiers proposes splitting the requirement in two — full-screen content such as video and games, where magnification is not expected, and everything else, where it is. mraccess77 adds that browser zoom is not assistive technology and that authors can read viewport scale.

positions.label: Zoom cannot be accounted for
positions.detail: GreggVan, who drove flashing into WCAG originally, states the intent was never that content be safe at arbitrary zoom — people with low vision also lean toward the screen, and no requirement can survive unbounded magnification. His central argument is cost: a 400% allowance would make the provision more than 10 times harder to pass while still not protecting every user, a rule that draconian would not be adopted by standards and regulatory bodies, and the real solution is display-time detection and prevention tools. alastc opened #631 saying that accounting for zoom removes all sizing assumptions, leaving only contrast and frequency, while acknowledging this misses the low vision plus epilepsy need; asked why GreggVan advised against shrinking the area, he named false positives: failing content that harms nobody, which may be an acceptable trade against seizures but is the main cost. bruce-usab doubts zoom can be factored in, and questions how a full-screen exception could be worded without being too broad to be useful.

positions.label: A warning is not a remedy
positions.detail: GreggVan's reductio — that WCAG could otherwise be replaced by a single site-wide "this site may not be suitable or safe for anyone with a disability" notice — drew a reply from patrickhlauke that the idea was a scoped exemption, not a carte blanche; GreggVan then allowed that content could meet a minimum standard by warning first, provided it is not called accessible. nattarnoff, who experiences these effects, says a warning makes them leave and look for an alternative rather than granting access. mraccess77 notes timestamps on a flashing video still do not deliver the missed information.

positions.label: A responsible warning can suffice
positions.detail: In #632 alastc relays Bruce's view that the common YouTuber protocol of a warning plus timestamps addresses the need and satisfies No Flashing through the user-preference note, and expects an exception or applies-when for flashing preceded by a warning. patrickhlauke reads this as an exemption for flashing often outside the author's control, conditional on a warning. In #631 bruce-usab agrees a generic up-front warning is not enough, but argues that a warning at the start and shortly before the flash, in educational content where the flashing is essential and audio description is provided, should be sufficient for WCAG3.

agreed: The flashing requirements and the separate flash-and-motion warning requirement have to be reconciled — #632 exists specifically to do that.
open: Whether the size threshold accounts for zoom, and whether to split full-screen from inline content.

Whether a user preference to prevent flashing can be relied on. alastc raised it, saying he does not think such a method is accessibility supported now, and relayed julierawe's comment that relying on it seems dangerous; the draft note applies only if such a method exists.

Whether responsibility for detecting and suppressing flashing sits with authors or with browsers — nattarnoff raised it; alastc noted the animation requirements are affected by the same user-preference question.

Whether a warning can count toward meeting the requirement or only supports a scoped exception — bruce-usab, patrickhlauke and alastc see a role for it, while GreggVan, nattarnoff and mraccess77 say a warning does not make the content accessible.

Whether flashing should be ruled out more broadly — WilcoFiers and detlevhfischer see little loss in avoiding it, while mraccess77 notes some users, such as a deaf user wanting audio alerts mirrored visually, may want safe flashing on purpose.

trigger-warning-available.headline: Whether a warning before flashing or motion can ever count toward passing, whether the provision's name misleads when the draft limits triggers to flashing, motion and pseudo-motion, and how far older proposals on mood and storylines filed under the same label should reach.

positions.label: A warning may suffice where an exemption exists
positions.detail: alastc opens #632 as a placeholder to make sure the updated flashing requirements work with the warning requirement, quoting Bruce's comment that YouTubers commonly warn about flashing and give time stamps, a protocol Bruce considers sufficient for the disability-related need and believes satisfies No Flashing via the note on accessibility-supported user preferences, though it takes a bit of rationalization. Bruce asks that the note, or the easily avoidable idea, be made explicit. alastc suggests an exception or applies-when clause will probably be needed. patrickhlauke reads the idea as exempting situations often outside the author's control as long as there is at least a warning first, but says the exemption must exist in the first place and is not a carte blanche.

positions.label: A warning does not make content accessible
positions.detail: GreggVan objects that counting a warning amounts to saying something is accessible if users are warned not to use it; warnings are good but should not count as passing that content. He later allows that the group can say a site meets its minimum standard if it warns first, or exclude content through an exception, as long as it is clear the content is not accessible. nattarnoff, who uses motion trigger warnings in presentations and is affected by such effects, says a warning should exist but is not sufficient: faced with one, nattarnoff leaves and looks for an alternative, and closing one's eyes for a few seconds usually means missing key content.

positions.label: The name misleads
positions.detail: sydneycolemanfromgoogle's #541 says the phrase trigger warning has a broader meaning and could be read as belonging to the Control possible harm - Triggers area, and asks for a more specific name or a different phrase. julierawe's #736, filed for the COGA Task Force, notes that trigger warnings usually concern emotional health, which makes the provision confusing when its note defines triggers as flashing, motion lasting more than 5 seconds, and pseudo-motion; it recommends renaming it "Motion warnings available".

positions.label: A defined list of common triggers is needed
positions.detail: In #542, supports the effort but says it requires a specific list of common triggers to be tagged; leaving the determination to products would produce wildly inconsistent results, and subjective guidelines could supplement such a list but not replace it.

positions.label: Extend warnings to mood and connotation
positions.detail: SuzanneKTaylor's #88 argues content can create a mood without containing any item identifiable as a trigger, and proposes that information about the mood content is likely to encourage be available or user-selectable, aimed at long-form content such as a movie, an ebook or a VR experience. medeaoblongata sees a related gap for connotative aspects of content, as distinct from denotative or purely decorative ones, where flagging a connotation can be more useful than a description.

positions.label: Mood is not measurable or auditable
positions.detail: detlevhfischer says mood depends on the user and context rather than being a property of content, that exposing annotations would add to cognitive load for many users, and that he does not see how it could become a general measurable outcome. ericwbailey says it would be impossible to quantify, before even considering cultural differences. patrickhlauke dreads auditors having to check this kind of meta information when judging conformance.

positions.label: Storylines, and subtle triggers left to AT
positions.detail: SuzanneKTaylor's #89 proposes that interwoven storylines be programmatically distinguishable or selectable, so some subtle triggers can be avoided by watching or skipping one full story. GreggVan replies that no content is free of triggers for everyone and that AI-based AT that detects and redacts per individual is the better route. SuzanneKTaylor agrees AT may handle these outcomes, with WCAG concerned with whether AT has the access it needs, but warns that a personal trigger profile could itself be triggering or harmful if leaked, so outcomes may need to stay at simple, common triggers for now.

agreed: Warnings themselves are worth providing — GreggVan calls them good and nattarnoff says there should be one; the dispute in #632 is whether they count toward passing.

Connotation annotations on images and alt text, the separate idea Brennan raised rather than the mood metadata proposal, would surface through a user agent, OS or screen reader setting rather than by default — detlevhfischer asked and SuzanneKTaylor confirmed.
open: Whether flashing or moving content preceded by a warning can pass through an exception or applies-when clause, as alastc suggests in #632, or whether a warning should never count, as GreggVan and nattarnoff argue.
Whether the provision is renamed, for example to "Motion warnings available" as the COGA Task Force proposes; #541 and #736 have no replies.
Whether WCAG 3 defines a list of common triggers to be tagged (#542), unanswered.
Whether mood belongs in WCAG at all or is an assistive-technology concern, and how it could be scoped for a conformance claim.
How AT would evaluate long-form content — SuzanneKTaylor's own question is whether it could judge a whole movie or would get stopped at the first ad.
trigger-warning-available.note: The provision text and its note limit triggers to flashing, motion lasting more than 5 seconds and pseudo-motion; #632 is the only thread with discussion of that provision as drafted, and #541, #542 and #736 are unanswered issue bodies. #88 and #89 are 2024 proposals by SuzanneKTaylor that predate the drafted provision and are shared with Safe content review.
